------------------------------------< Abstract >----------------------------------------

This study examines how firms can strategically integrate rapidly evolving artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities

with growing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) imperatives. Addressing the critical yet understudied

challenge of aligning technological innovation with sustainability objectives, we propose two novel frameworks:

AI-led ESG, enabling AI-advanced firms to strategically leverage technology for sustainability, and ESG-led AI,

guiding resource-constrained SMEs toward incremental AI adoption aligned with ESG goals. Using illustrative

cases from manufacturing, molding, and textiles, we demonstrate how strategic AI deployment enhances ESG

performance, driving sustainable innovation, competitiveness, and long-term resilience. We further reveal that

proactive alignment between ESG and AI not only mitigates sustainability risks but also unlocks previously

untapped market opportunities. Ultimately, we emphasize that clear governance, supportive policy contexts, and

innovation-oriented cultures are critical for successful ESG-AI integration, providing actionable strategic insights

for both theory and practice.

Keywords: AI-led ESG, ESG-led AI, SMEs, Sustainable Development, ESG Management

I. Introduction

Growing  global  attention  to  climate change, human  rights,  labor  standards, and

transparent governance has significantly elevated expectations for corporate sustainability

(Asif, Searcy, & Castka, 2023; Lim, 2024). While initially directed at large multinational

corporations, these heightened environmental, social, and governance (ESG) demands now

increasingly affect small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), challenging their global

competitiveness (Burnaev, Mironov, Shpilman, Mironenko, & Katalevsky, 2023; Dunne &

McBrayer, 2019). Concurrently, rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) raise a

critical yet unresolved question: How can firms—especially resource-constrained SMEs—

effectively leverage AI to respond strategically to ESG imperatives?

Firms have typically viewed AI as a tool to automate routine operations. However,

recent research reveals AI’s potential extends beyond efficiency, enabling real-time

resource  monitoring,  enhanced  governance  transparency,  and  improved   ethical

decision-making (Nishant, Kennedy, & Corbett, 2020; Rane, Choudhary, & Rane, 2024).

Such capabilities allow SMEs to achieve ESG outcomes previously limited to larger firms

(Chen, Wang, Lin, Liu, & Hu, 2024). Yet, an important but overlooked distinction persists

between  SMEs  that  adopt  AI  reactively  in  response  to  ESG  pressures  and

technology-driven firms proactively using AI to strengthen ESG initiatives. Reactive firms

often lack sufficient data infrastructure, technical expertise, and organizational readiness,

whereas proactive firms strategically leverage existing AI capabilities to enhance ethics,

stakeholder  engagement,  and  ESG  compliance  effectiveness  (Ghobakhloo,  Asadi,

Iranmanesh, Foroughi, Mubarak, & Yadegaridehkordi, 2023). Recognizing this distinction

raises a critical question: How can different types of firms strategically harness AI to

realize meaningful ESG outcomes?

To address this question, we propose two novel frameworks: AI-led ESG and ESG-led

AI. These frameworks offer actionable guidance tailored to firms’ technological contexts,

clarifying how organizations can leverage AI  strategically to achieve ESG  goals. By

exploring this intersection, we contribute a clearer understanding of how firms integrate

advanced  technologies  with  sustainability  imperatives,  highlighting pathways  toward

long-term competitiveness and sustainable innovation.

In  particular, recent  industry-specific evidence  illustrates the  versatility of AI  in

meeting ESG imperatives (e.g., carbon-intensive industries: Crocco, Broccardo, Alofaysan,

& Agarwal, 2024; FinTech: Kazachenok, Stankevich, Chubaeva, & Tyurina, 2023). In

textiles, firms leverage AI to minimize waste, optimize raw material use, and enhance

workplace safety.  In manufacturing, smart factories employ AI for real-time energy

management, predictive maintenance, and automated quality assurance. Similarly, molding

firms also adopt AI-based precision machining and on-demand production to reduce

material usage and costs. Despite these promising examples, SMEs typically adopt AI

reactively due to infrastructure limitations and talent shortages, thus failing to integrate

AI strategically into ESG frameworks. Addressing this gap, our study proposes a strategic

framework  guiding SMEs  toward  proactive,  AI-driven  digital  transformation  (DX).

Specifically, we clarify conceptual differences between firms using AI merely to comply

with ESG pressures versus those proactively employing AI to strengthen existing ESG

initiatives, and provide practical solutions for overcoming technological and organizational

barriers (Li, Wu, Hu, Pan, & Zhou, 2025).

Ultimately,  this paper argues  that  strategic  integration of AI and ESG enhances

corporate  competitiveness  and  ensures  long-term  industry   viability  (Minkkinen,

Niukkanen, & Mäntymäki, 2024). Rather than viewing ESG as a compliance expense, firms

should embrace  it as a transformative investment that balances immediate gains with

long-term resilience (Agapova & Garanina, 2024; Wang, Jiao, & Ma, 2024). By integrating

ESG considerations into AI adoption—thereby forging AI-led ESG and ESG-led AI—SMEs

can  cultivate  sustainable growth  strategies  benefiting  companies,  stakeholders, and

society. This research offers a practical roadmap for scholars, industry practitioners, and

policymakers aiming to support SMEs in meeting emerging global sustainability challenges.

II. Theoretical Background

2.1 AI in SMEs and Startups

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) within small and medium-sized enterprises

(SMEs) and startups presents distinct opportunities and notable challenges. On the positive

side, AI’s  capacity  to  automate  processes  and  analyze  data  empowers  smaller

organizations to foster innovation, enhance productivity, and achieve economies of scale

(Iyelolu, Agu, Idemudia, & Ijomah, 2024). For example, various SMEs in manufacturing

have documented significant improvements in product quality and operational efficiency

by embedding AI solutions into their production lines (Peretz-Andersson, Tabares, Mikalef,

& Parida, 2024). Moreover, AI-focused startups have attracted substantial venture capital

interest, largely because their disruptive technologies can swiftly reshape established

markets (Bammens & Hünermund, 2021).

However, several barriers inhibit AI adoption among smaller firms. Chief among these

are  financial  and human  capital  constraints,  limiting  investment  in  robust  data

infrastructures and the recruitment of specialized AI talent. A McKinsey study identifies

resource  scarcity  as a  primary  challenge  specifically  facing  manufacturing  SMEs.

Additionally,  SMEs   often   lack   sufficient   high-quality   datasets  and   effective

data-management practices, both essential for training reliable AI models (Chui, Manyika,

Miremadi, Henke, Chung, Nel, & Malhotra, 2018; Lamarre, Smaje, & Zemmel, 2023).

Furthermore, successful digital transformation (DX) requires committed leadership and an

organizational culture supportive of experimentation. Yet, SMEs frequently  prioritize

immediate   revenue   generation   over   long-term   technological   competitiveness,

undervaluing AI’s strategic importance (Burnaev et  al., 2023). Reflecting this reality,

nearly half of small enterprises surveyed reported having no immediate plans for AI

adoption.

Ethical and risk management concerns pose additional hurdles. Smaller organizations

generally have less formal oversight mechanisms to guard against algorithmic bias, opaque

decision processes, or cybersecurity threats (Bughin, Hazan, Sree Ramaswamy, & Chu,

2017).  Nevertheless,  the  emergence  of  no-code  and  low-code  AI  platforms  and

cloud-based AI application programming interfaces (APIs) reduces the technical barrier to

implementing  AI. By leveraging these newer tools—often complemented by targeted

training programs, government subsidies, or open-source solutions—SMEs and startups can

more feasibly integrate AI into their operations (Khan, Taherdoost, Madanchian, Ouaissa,

El Hajjami, & Rahman, 2024). Thus, while AI holds considerable promise for bolstering

competitiveness and aligning with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) objectives,

clear strategies and external support remain vital for successful adoption.

2.2 Convergence of AI and ESG

Building on the discussion of AI adoption in SMEs and startups, the intersection of

artificial intelligence (AI) with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) objectives

underscores a broader paradigmatic shift in how organizations perceive and implement

sustainability.  Rather  than  viewing ESG  as a  peripheral  compliance  requirement,

companies  increasingly  recognize  AI  as a  strategic instrument  that can  streamline

operational processes while fostering ethical accountability. In line with stakeholder theory

(Freeman, 2010) and the triple bottom line (Elkington, 1997), ESG-driven initiatives are

no longer confined to risk mitigation; they also embody opportunities for shared value

creation (Porter & Kramer, 2011). This section examines the conceptual rationale behind

AI-ESG integration, explores domain-specific applications, highlights the role of emerging

digital technologies in augmenting ESG  efforts, and discusses  limitations and  ethical

considerations.

2.2.1. The Rationale for AI-ESG Convergence

The  growing  emphasis on  environmental,  social, and governance  (ESG)  standards,

reinforced by frameworks such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),

highlights a fundamental  shift toward aligning organizational success with  societal and

environmental objectives. Simultaneously,  artificial  intelligence  (AI) has emerged as a

transformative means to support these objectives through data-driven decision-making.

This convergence between AI and ESG involves strategically integrating AI’s predictive,

optimization,  and  automation  capabilities  with ESG’s  sustainability  goals  across

environmental, social, and governance domains. Specifically, AI helps operationalize ESG by

translating abstract sustainability goals into measurable outcomes. For example, predictive

modeling and real-time monitoring technologies enable firms to accurately track resource

use and  emissions,  turning  qualitative ESG commitments  into  quantifiable  indicators

(Bebbington & Unerman, 2018). This  capability  is  particularly valuable for small and

medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which often lack resources to effectively pursue ESG

initiatives (Li et al., 2025). Responsibly implemented AI can thus enhance efficiency, reduce

operational costs, and strengthen stakeholder trust by providing verifiable ESG data.

Conceptually, this AI-ESG integration aligns closely with dynamic capabilities theory

(Teece,  Pisano, &  Shuen,  1997),  which  highlights  organizations'  abilities  to  adapt

strategically  in dynamic  environments. By  leveraging  AI,  firms can  better  identify

ESG-related  risks and  opportunities,  seize data-informed  strategies, and reconfigure

processes to meet sustainability demands. However, successfully converging AI and ESG

requires proactive ethical leadership. The strategic value of AI depends not only on

performance  optimization  but  equally  on  embedding  transparency,  fairness,  and

accountability into organizational systems (Burnaev et al., 2023). Leaders must ensure AI

adoption aligns with ethical standards—such as the OECD AI Principles or the EU’s

Ethics  Guidelines  for  Trustworthy AI—to  prevent  biases,  exclusion,  or  unintended

consequences that might ultimately undermine ESG goals.

2.2.2. Domain-Specific Applications

In practice, AI’s impact on ESG dimensions manifests differently across environmental,

social, and governance domains. In the environmental sphere, AI-driven solutions—such as

machine learning models integrated with satellite imagery or Industrial Internet of Things

(IoT)  sensors—facilitate  real-time  tracking of  emissions,  predictive maintenance, and

adaptive energy management. In particular, these tools enable proactive interventions that

reduce waste and carbon footprints, as  illustrated by manufacturing firms achieving

significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions (Lim, 2024). Social applications are

equally expansive. AI can promote fairness in hiring and promotion by identifying potential

biases through advanced analytics, and improve workplace safety by monitoring employee

well-being in high-risk environments (Ghobakhloo et al., 2023).

In governance, anomaly detection algorithms help preempt financial misreporting and

fraud,  while  chatbots  and  other  automated  tools  promote  consistent,  transparent

stakeholder  engagement. These  domain-specific  applications  align  closely  with  the

resource-based view  (Barney,  1991),  highlighting how  intangible assets—such as AI

capabilities and reputational capital from ESG leadership—serve as critical sources of

sustained  competitive advantage  (Zeng,  Yunis,  Khalil, &  Mirza,  2024). To  illustrate

Moreover, integrating AI with big data, IoT, and blockchain significantly enhances ESG

initiatives. IoT sensors in factories and logistics networks provide real-time data on energy

use, waste generation, and workplace safety. AI algorithms analyze this data instantly,

enabling timely responses to inefficiencies or risks. For example, textile manufacturers

can combine temperature and humidity sensor data with production analytics to optimize

energy consumption and minimize fabric waste, generating operational savings aligned

with shared value creation (Ministry of SMEs and Startups, 2025).

At the same time, blockchain technology offers a secure, tamper-resistant platform for

storing and verifying ESG-related information. This  is particularly beneficial in supply

chain contexts, where ethical sourcing and transparent recordkeeping are top priorities.

An AI-enabled system can detect anomalies in supplier data—indicating possible unethical

labor practices or incorrect emissions reporting—and automatically log these findings on

a blockchain ledger. This approach deters greenwashing and supports compliance with

emerging standards, such as Integrated Reporting and the Task Force on Climate-related

Financial Disclosures (Miglionico, 2022). Together, these emerging technologies enhance

the precision,  scalability, and credibility of ESG initiatives, opening new frontiers for

established corporations and resource-constrained SMEs.

2.2.3. Risks and Ethical Considerations

Despite its promise, AI-led ESG carries inherent challenges that must be addressed to

ensure equitable and sustainable outcomes. For SMEs and startups,  limited  financial

resources and human capital often hamper the development of robust AI infrastructures,

reflecting structural barriers recognized in resource dependence theory (Pfeffer; 1987;

Pfeffer & Salancik,  2015). Furthermore, data-related complexities—ranging from the

availability of  large,  high-quality datasets to stringent data privacy regulations—can

impede model accuracy and regulatory compliance.

Ethical risks also persist, particularly concerning algorithmic bias. If training data lack

diversity or reflect historical inequities, AI systems may perpetuate discriminatory patterns,

thereby undermining progress on the social dimension of ESG (Guan, Dong, & Zhao, 2022;

Minkkinen et al., 2024). Cybersecurity represents another critical area of concern, given

the extensive data interchange required by AI-driven ESG systems (Zeng et al., 2024).

As IoT sensors and blockchain networks expand, firms face heightened risks of data

breaches or malicious tampering, potentially compromising proprietary information and

undermining  public  trust  in ESG  disclosures (Minkkinen et  al.,  2024). Consequently,

organizations must strengthen data governance through secure frameworks and clear

accountability structures, such as cross-functional oversight committees, internal audits,

and adherence to standards like ISO 27001 for information security. In short, integrating

AI with ESG signals a strategic shift from compliance toward embedding sustainability into

core decision-making processes. By leveraging AI’s predictive and analytical capabilities,

firms  can  proactively  address  inefficiencies,  enhance  social  welfare,  and  ensure

transparent governance (Iyelolu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024).

2.3 Adopting AI for ESG versus Enhancing ESG in AI-Based Firms

Building on the previous analysis, this section explores two distinct yet complementary

strategic approaches: (1) adopting AI primarily to achieve ESG goals and (2) enhancing

ESG practices in firms with advanced AI  capabilities. Although both leverage AI for

sustainable outcomes,  their  motivations,  challenges, and  benefits  differ  significantly,

especially for SMEs and startups. The key differences between these strategies are

2.3.1. Strategy of Adopting AI for ESG

Effectively integrating AI into ESG initiatives requires a strategic approach addressing

three interrelated dimensions: data infrastructure, specialized talent, and organizational

culture.  First, organizations must develop robust data systems capable of accurately

capturing ESG-related metrics. Manufacturing firms, for instance, might deploy sensors to

track energy use and material waste, while financial institutions aggregate ESG indicators

across investment portfolios. Analyzing such datasets through machine learning and deep

learning  methods  can  provide  actionable  insights  for  strategic  decision-making

(Peretz-Andersson et al., 2024).

Second, successful AI-ESG integration depends on securing professionals with expertise

in both AI technologies and sustainability. Increasingly, firms are aligning analytics teams

closely with Chief Sustainability Officers (CSOs) or forming partnerships with external AI

specialists to bridge existing capability gaps  (Asif et  al., 2023). Third, cultivating an

ESG-centric  organizational  culture  is  essential.  Leaders must  actively champion  AI

adoption, clearly communicate its strategic importance, and allocate sufficient resources

for experimentation and learning. Although integrating AI involves iterative  trial and

error,  a  committed  leadership  approach  helps   institutionalize  data-driven  ESG

decision-making, ultimately enhancing operational efficiency and sustainability outcomes

(Florea & Croitoru, 2025).

While  the  initial  investment  in  technology,  talent, and  cultural change can be

substantial, organizations effectively adopting AI for ESG initiatives strengthen investor

trust  and  market  credibility  (Minkkinen  et   al.,  2024).  For  example,  traditional

manufacturers  using  AI-driven energy management systems can  significantly lower

carbon emissions and transparently report their progress to stakeholders (Ali, Motuzienė,

& Džiugaitė-Tumėnienė, 2024). SMEs facing resource constraints can begin by adopting

cloud-based AI solutions or partnering with external consultants, gradually scaling their

capabilities to achieve measurable ESG outcomes. Ultimately, aligning digital investment

strategies  with ESG governance  not  only advances  sustainability agendas  but  also

promotes long-term operational excellence (Khan et al., 2024).

2.3.2. AI-Based Companies Enhancing ESG Strategy

In contrast, organizations rooted in AI typically have ESG principles more intrinsically

embedded in their products. Because they already excel in data analytics and algorithmic

innovation, their ESG frameworks tend to be proactive and tightly integrated. First, these

companies often establish ethical AI guidelines to address potential biases, ensure data

privacy, and maintain transparency. For instance, a large-scale AI solution provider might

form an ethics committee to assess societal risks, publish transparent documentation, and

implement  oversight  mechanisms  that  strengthen  governance  accountability   (Li,

Hammoud, Itani, Khizbullin, & Ghanem, 2023).

Second, creating social and environmental value emerges as a strategic priority. By

developing carbon-tracking software or specialized ESG assessment tools, AI-driven firms

capitalize on their technical strengths while advancing sustainability objectives. Many

startups operate with a dual positioning: as a green tech company that attracts socially

conscious customers and investors. (Crocco et  al., 2024). Third, sustainable operations

represent a  critical dimension. Because AI companies often maintain extensive data

centers,  incorporating renewable energy  sources  or  offsetting  emissions  is key  to

long-term viability. Major technology enterprises like Microsoft and Google have publicly

committed to solar and wind power investments, supplemented by carbon credits, in

pursuit of carbon neutrality (Shrimali, 2022). They also adopt green procurement and

waste reduction practices, extending environmental criteria to suppliers and addressing

Scope 3 emissions*.

Finally, transparent data disclosure and stakeholder engagement ensure that AI-based

enterprises maintain consistent governance standards. Historically, technology companies

have been cautious in revealing proprietary information, but ESG pressures drive more

openness—including support for open-source  projects,  clear algorithmic  policies, and

publicly available model evaluations (Khan et  al., 2024; Miglionico, 2022). Early-stage

startups  also  benefit from  articulating  social  missions and  publishing ESG  reports,

reinforcing investor confidence and differentiating themselves in a competitive market

(Mansouri & Momtaz, 2022). By weaving ESG into their core strategies, AI-oriented firms

can more readily adapt to regulatory changes, attract mission-aligned capital, and sustain

a competitive edge through responsible innovation.

2.3.3. Comparing the Viewpoints of SMEs and Startups

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and startups rarely adopt standardized

III. Strategic Models for ESG-AI Integration

tech-focused startups or firms  proficient  in  AI, leveraging  existing competencies to

3.1 ESG-led AI Strategy Model

An  ESG-led  AI  approach  begins  by  evaluating  current ESG  performance  and

technological readiness. SMEs  typically assess environmental metrics such as energy

efficiency, carbon emissions, and waste management; social factors like labor practices

and community  involvement; and governance  aspects  including  internal  ethics and

compliance processes (Smith, Schäfer, & Bernstein, 2024). Based on this assessment, firms

conduct a gap analysis to pinpoint areas where targeted AI interventions can achieve

meaningful ESG improvements.

Implementing this strategy involves deploying specific AI  tools, such as IoT-driven

energy management, machine vision for optimized production, or NLP for employee

engagement  analytics  (Ali  et  al.,  2024; Crocco  et  al.,  2024). Given  limited  internal

expertise, SMEs  frequently leverage  external  partnerships  or  incrementally develop

in-house  AI  capabilities.  Essential  infrastructural elements  include cloud-based data

storage, secure governance frameworks, and real-time analytics capabilities. Pilot projects

typically focus on high-impact ESG areas—for example, predictive energy optimization or

sensor-based workplace safety monitoring—and are gradually scaled upon successful

outcomes (Rane et al., 2024).

Sustaining ESG-led AI  efforts requires  clearly defined KPIs, transparent AI-driven

reporting, strong leadership commitment, employee training, and continuous refinement of

AI applications (Blank, Sgambati, & Truelson, 2016). This approach effectively integrates

ESG  principles  into core business  operations,  ultimately strengthening  organizational

sustainability and competitiveness.

3.2 AI-led ESG Strategy Model

The AI-led ESG approach emphasizes embedding responsible AI (RAI) governance

structures to proactively manage ethical,  social, and governance risks (Lu, Zhu, Xu,

Whittle, Zowghi, & Jacquet, 2024), particularly in tech-focused SMEs and startups with

established AI infrastructure. Ethical oversight mechanisms, such as data governance

boards or ethics committees, address algorithmic bias, data privacy, and transparency

throughout AI deployment, strengthening stakeholder trust (Guan et al., 2022).

These AI-centric firms often deploy their capabilities directly toward significant social

and  environmental  challenges.  AI-driven  diagnostic  tools,  personalized  educational

technologies, environmental monitoring through computer vision, or predictive analytics

for disaster mitigation illustrate this proactive approach. Real-world examples include

deploying NLP  analytics  to measure  public  policy  sentiment  or  using drone-based

computer vision to monitor deforestation (Verma, 2022), each providing tangible societal

benefits and new market opportunities (Bebbington & Unerman, 2018).

Furthermore, sustainable operations are essential for AI-intensive organizations due to

their large computational demands. Companies like Google have harnessed AI to optimize

data center cooling systems, achieving approximately 40% energy savings (Karunakara

Malige & Ananth, 2024). Additional sustainability practices—such as renewable energy

sourcing, waste-heat recovery, and efficient computing architectures—underscore how

operational excellence can align with environmental responsibility (Miglionico, 2022; Smith

et al., 2024).

For these reasons, transparent, data-driven governance  is  critical for AI-led ESG

organizations. Automated ESG  reporting and  real-time  risk monitoring  help reduce

potential harms while enhancing responsiveness, and clear disclosure protocols bolster

trust among investors, consumers, and regulatory bodies. Effective crisis communication

and accountability measures reinforce ethical standards, ensuring AI’s transformative

power contributes to business success and societal benefit.

3.3 Comparative Analysis of ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG

Although both ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG approaches integrate ESG criteria with AI

technologies, they differ significantly in motivation and operational focus. ESG-led AI

adopts a top-down perspective, starting from clearly defined sustainability goals and

employing AI solutions to realize them. Conversely, AI-led ESG leverages existing AI

infrastructure, subsequently embedding ESG considerations into operations and ethics

frameworks (Chen et  al., 2024; Nishant et  al., 2020). Practical industry cases highlight

these strategic differences (Ministry of SMEs and Startups, 2025), as illustrated in <Figure 2>.

1. Manufacturing Industry (ESG-led AI): A metal parts producer introduced IoT sensors

and a predictive maintenance algorithm, reducing overall energy consumption by 20%,

minimizing raw material waste, and improving operational throughput.  Initially, limited

digital literacy and resistance to new technology required targeted training and external

partnerships. Over several months, the pilot project scaled across multiple production

lines, illustrating how a top-down ESG focus can drive steady, long-term improvements.

2. Textile Industry (ESG-led  AI): A garment manufacturing SME adopted AI-driven

demand forecasting and defect detection, cutting fabric waste by 10% and enhancing

quality control. These incremental gains fostered a more positive work environment, as

employees benefited from safer schedules and clearer performance metrics. This example

underscores how incremental AI adoption can effectively address both economic and

social dimensions of ESG.

3. Tech  Industry  (AI-led ESG): A data  analytics  startup  utilizes  natural language

processing  (NLP)  to  automate ESG  risk  assessments,  enhancing  transparency and

stakeholder communication. Meanwhile, Google’s AI-based data center optimizations

achieved up to 40% reductions in cooling energy, aligning operational efficiency with

environmental objectives. These examples show how preexisting AI infrastructures can

deliver  swift,  high-impact  results—provided  there  is  robust  ethical  oversight  and

stakeholder engagement to prevent unintended consequences (Kazachenok et al., 2023).

IV. Conclusion

4.1 Summary

This  study has examined two  strategic models  for  integrating  sustainability and

technological innovation: ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG. Although both frameworks seek to

align environmental, social, and governance (ESG) principles with artificial intelligence

(AI), their starting points differ  significantly. ESG-led AI entails building responsible,

transparent AI  solutions to meet  stringent ESG requirements, making  it  particularly

suitable  for  organizations—often  small and medium-sized  enterprises (SMEs)—whose

digital infrastructures remain underdeveloped (Minkkinen et al., 2024; Peretz-Andersson,

et al., 2024) In contrast, AI-led ESG leverages well-established AI competencies to address

ESG challenges more immediately, favoring tech-driven interventions that can rapidly

scale. Viewed in tandem, these models underscore AI’s expanding function as a force

for resilience and long-term societal value, well beyond mere operational efficiency

<Figure 3>.

<Figure 3> Summary of ESG-Led AI and AI-Led ESG

From  a  policy  and  practical  perspective,  the  findings  highlight  three  critical

interventions to foster an enabling environment for both ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG.

First, tailored support for SMEs—through specialized training, consulting subsidies, or

targeted tax incentives—can alleviate the financial and human capital constraints they

frequently encounter. Such measures not only lower  initial adoption costs but  also

promote phased implementation of AI tools, ensuring that ESG objectives remain central

during digital transformation (Blank et al., 2016; He, 2024).

Second, establishing and enforcing robust AI ethics guidelines helps avert algorithmic

bias, data misuse, and opaque decision-making processes (Agapova & Garanina, 2024).

When developed collaboratively by governments, industry associations, and academic

institutions, these guidelines serve as guardrails that bolster public trust and steer AI

deployments toward equitable, socially beneficial outcomes (Iyelolu et al., 2024; Mansouri

& Momtaz, 2022).

Finally, mandatory ESG disclosure provides the transparency essential for effective

AI-driven analyses. By requiring firms to report on emissions,  social  initiatives, and

governance   practices,  policymakers  reduce   information  asymmetry,   discourage

greenwashing, and enable stakeholders to accurately evaluate corporate ESG performance

(Chui et  al., 2018; Kazachenok et  al., 2024). Operationally, ESG-led AI often involves

incrementally enhancing existing processes—such as energy management or supply-chain

monitoring—by integrating AI solutions that optimize resource usage, identify anomalies,

or  predict emerging  risks.  In contrast, AI-led ESG enables firms with advanced AI

capabilities to pursue more ambitious  initiatives, such as developing low-carbon data

centers or deploying predictive analytics for community health.

Despite these differences, the core message remains consistent: AI can become the

linchpin of ethical and sustainable corporate transformation, provided robust governance

structures, committed leadership, and transparent stakeholder engagement are in place.

Building on stakeholder theory (Freeman, 2010) and dynamic capabilities (Teece et  al.,

1997), the strategic models in this study demonstrate that embedding ESG within AI—and

AI within ESG can generate a virtuous cycle of innovation and accountability.

Moreover, recognizing the complementary nature of these two approaches underscores

an important theme: synergistic integration. Even tech-savvy startups can learn from

ESG-led AI’s  methodical  emphasis  on  ethics  and  responsible  governance,  while

traditional SMEs adopting ESG-led AI can benefit from the scalability and agility that

characterize AI-led ESG. Over time, organizations may transition between or combine

these  models,  forging  hybrid  strategies  that  unite  gradual  capacity-building  with

disruptive, high-impact solutions (Florea & Croitoru, 2025). This fluidity not only amplifies

ESG outcomes but also reinforces public trust, attracting mission-aligned investors and

galvanizing broader stakeholder support.

For SMEs  in  particular, external  policy  incentives and a step-by-step  integration

strategy can mitigate  financial and  technical  barriers, transforming short-term  pilot

programs into long-term competitive advantages (Khan et  al., 2024; Chui et  al., 2018).

Ultimately, whether an organization initiates its journey with ESG-led AI or AI-led ESG,

the end goal converges on responsible digital innovation—an imperative in an era where

environmental constraints, social well-being, and governance expectations are redefining

global  market  dynamics.  By  uniting  technological  excellence  with  sustainability

imperatives, firms can ensure that AI’s transformative capabilities not only enhance

operational efficiency but also foster equitable growth and ecological stewardship for

future generations (Bammens & Hünermund, 2021).

4.2 Limitation and Future Research

Despite the promise of ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG,  this study’s findings remain

conceptual  and  partially  illustrated  through  selective  case  examples  rather  than

comprehensive  empirical  data.  First, the  lack of  large-scale,  data-driven  validation

presents a key limitation. Researchers could undertake longitudinal or cross-sectional

studies in multiple industries to quantify how AI adoption directly or indirectly affects ESG

performance over time. Such analyses would elucidate best practices, uncover potential

trade-offs, and provide tangible evidence for policymakers and corporate strategists.

Second, an industry-specific focus dominated many existing discussions, spotlighting

sectors like finance and high-tech (Asif et al., 2023). Future research should explore how

these dual models function in diverse environments—including manufacturing, healthcare,

and the public sector—where operational processes and stakeholder complexities differ

markedly. Such breadth would deepen our understanding of the conditions under which

ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG thrive or falter.

Third, the rapid pace of  technological and regulatory change  calls  for  continual

updating of theoretical frameworks and governance mechanisms (Wu, Straub, & Liang,

2015). Dynamic  regulatory landscapes and emerging AI innovations—from federated

learning  to  quantum  computing—require  agile,  adaptive  strategies.  Scholars  and

practitioners may investigate how real-time policy adjustments and advanced governance

protocols could strengthen ethical oversight and ESG impacts (Nishant et al., 2020).

Finally, the combined implementation of ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG represents a

promising yet underexplored area for empirical study. Although theory suggests that

organizations applying both models simultaneously or sequentially may achieve superior

outcomes, systematic evaluations of this synergy relative to singular strategies remain

limited (Acquaah & Yasai-Ardekani, 2008). Empirical validation could guide organizations

in  effectively  integrating  responsible  AI  practices  with ESG  objectives,  informing

standards and advancing sustainable digital transformation. Exploring these opportunities

can enhance theoretical clarity on ESG–AI integration, offering practical, evidence-based

insights for policymakers, firms, and communities pursuing ethical and sustainable AI

adoption.

‘AI 주도 ESG, ESG 주도 AI’

지속가능 경영을 위한 AI와 ESG의 전략적 융합 연구

하호정*, 정태연**, 구인혁***

본 연구는 인공지능(AI) 기술과 환경·사회·지배구조(ESG)의 전략적 결합을 통해 기업의 지속 가능

한 변화를 이끄는 두 가지 접근법을 제시하고, 각 전략의 강점과 한계를 평가한다. 첫 번째 전략인 'ESG

주도 AI (ESG-led AI)'는 ESG 목표를 설정한 후, 이를 실현할 수 있는 기술적 역량을 구축하고 AI 기술을

전략적으로 활용하는 방식이다. 이 전략은 ESG 목표달성에 집중하여 구체적인 성과를 낼 수 있다는

강점이 있으나, 기술 인프라 구축에 따른 비용 부담과 AI 전문성 부족이라는 한계를 지닌다. 두 번째

전략인 'AI 주도 ESG (AI-led ESG)'는 이미 AI 역량을 확보한 기술 중심 기업이 ESG 원칙을 조직 전반에

내재화하고, 윤리적 운영과 투명한 데이터 관리를 통해 ESG 성과를 창출하는 방식이다. 이 전략은 빠르

고 혁신적인 ESG 가치 창출이 가능하다는 장점이 있지만, AI를 활용하는 과정에서 윤리적 리스크와 복

잡한 규제 준수가 도전 과제로 부각된다. 따라서, 본 연구에서는 중소기업과 스타트업의 특수한 환경을

반영하여 두 전략의 실행 가능성을 이론적 분석과 실제 산업 사례를 통해 비교하고, 기업의 현실적 여

건에 맞는 실천적 시사점과 가이드라인을 제시한다. 결론적으로 AI와 ESG의 효과적 통합을 위해서는

명확한 내부 거버넌스 체계 구축, 혁신 지향적 조직문화 조성, 그리고 지속적인 교육과 정부의 정책적

지원이 필수적임을 강조한다.

This study examines how firms can strategically integrate rapidly evolving artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities

with growing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) imperatives. Addressing the critical yet understudied

challenge of aligning technological innovation with sustainability objectives, we propose two novel frameworks:

AI-led ESG, enabling AI-advanced firms to strategically leverage technology for sustainability, and ESG-led AI,

guiding resource-constrained SMEs toward incremental AI adoption aligned with ESG goals. Using illustrative

cases from manufacturing, molding, and textiles, we demonstrate how strategic AI deployment enhances ESG

performance, driving sustainable innovation, competitiveness, and long-term resilience. We further reveal that

proactive alignment between ESG and AI not only mitigates sustainability risks but also unlocks previously

untapped market opportunities. Ultimately, we emphasize that clear governance, supportive policy contexts, and

innovation-oriented cultures are critical for successful ESG-AI integration, providing actionable strategic insights

for both theory and practice.

Keywords: AI-led ESG, ESG-led AI, SMEs, Sustainable Development, ESG Management

sections.title: I. Introduction
sections.content:
Growing  global  attention  to  climate change, human  rights,  labor  standards, and

transparent governance has significantly elevated expectations for corporate sustainability

(Asif, Searcy, & Castka, 2023; Lim, 2024). While initially directed at large multinational

corporations, these heightened environmental, social, and governance (ESG) demands now

increasingly affect small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), challenging their global

competitiveness (Burnaev, Mironov, Shpilman, Mironenko, & Katalevsky, 2023; Dunne &

McBrayer, 2019). Concurrently, rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) raise a

critical yet unresolved question: How can firms—especially resource-constrained SMEs—

effectively leverage AI to respond strategically to ESG imperatives?

Firms have typically viewed AI as a tool to automate routine operations. However,

recent research reveals AI’s potential extends beyond efficiency, enabling real-time

resource  monitoring,  enhanced  governance  transparency,  and  improved   ethical

decision-making (Nishant, Kennedy, & Corbett, 2020; Rane, Choudhary, & Rane, 2024).

Such capabilities allow SMEs to achieve ESG outcomes previously limited to larger firms

(Chen, Wang, Lin, Liu, & Hu, 2024). Yet, an important but overlooked distinction persists

between  SMEs  that  adopt  AI  reactively  in  response  to  ESG  pressures  and

technology-driven firms proactively using AI to strengthen ESG initiatives. Reactive firms

often lack sufficient data infrastructure, technical expertise, and organizational readiness,

whereas proactive firms strategically leverage existing AI capabilities to enhance ethics,

stakeholder  engagement,  and  ESG  compliance  effectiveness  (Ghobakhloo,  Asadi,

Iranmanesh, Foroughi, Mubarak, & Yadegaridehkordi, 2023). Recognizing this distinction

raises a critical question: How can different types of firms strategically harness AI to

realize meaningful ESG outcomes?

To address this question, we propose two novel frameworks: AI-led ESG and ESG-led

AI. These frameworks offer actionable guidance tailored to firms’ technological contexts,

clarifying how organizations can leverage AI  strategically to achieve ESG  goals. By

exploring this intersection, we contribute a clearer understanding of how firms integrate

advanced  technologies  with  sustainability  imperatives,  highlighting pathways  toward

long-term competitiveness and sustainable innovation.

In  particular, recent  industry-specific evidence  illustrates the  versatility of AI  in

meeting ESG imperatives (e.g., carbon-intensive industries: Crocco, Broccardo, Alofaysan,

& Agarwal, 2024; FinTech: Kazachenok, Stankevich, Chubaeva, & Tyurina, 2023). In

textiles, firms leverage AI to minimize waste, optimize raw material use, and enhance

workplace safety.  In manufacturing, smart factories employ AI for real-time energy

management, predictive maintenance, and automated quality assurance. Similarly, molding

firms also adopt AI-based precision machining and on-demand production to reduce

material usage and costs. Despite these promising examples, SMEs typically adopt AI

reactively due to infrastructure limitations and talent shortages, thus failing to integrate

AI strategically into ESG frameworks. Addressing this gap, our study proposes a strategic

framework  guiding SMEs  toward  proactive,  AI-driven  digital  transformation  (DX).

Specifically, we clarify conceptual differences between firms using AI merely to comply

with ESG pressures versus those proactively employing AI to strengthen existing ESG

initiatives, and provide practical solutions for overcoming technological and organizational

barriers (Li, Wu, Hu, Pan, & Zhou, 2025).

Ultimately,  this paper argues  that  strategic  integration of AI and ESG enhances

corporate  competitiveness  and  ensures  long-term  industry   viability  (Minkkinen,

Niukkanen, & Mäntymäki, 2024). Rather than viewing ESG as a compliance expense, firms

should embrace  it as a transformative investment that balances immediate gains with

long-term resilience (Agapova & Garanina, 2024; Wang, Jiao, & Ma, 2024). By integrating

ESG considerations into AI adoption—thereby forging AI-led ESG and ESG-led AI—SMEs

can  cultivate  sustainable growth  strategies  benefiting  companies,  stakeholders, and

society. This research offers a practical roadmap for scholars, industry practitioners, and

policymakers aiming to support SMEs in meeting emerging global sustainability challenges.

sections.title: II. Theoretical Background
sections.content:
2.1 AI in SMEs and Startups

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) within small and medium-sized enterprises

(SMEs) and startups presents distinct opportunities and notable challenges. On the positive

side, AI’s  capacity  to  automate  processes  and  analyze  data  empowers  smaller

organizations to foster innovation, enhance productivity, and achieve economies of scale

(Iyelolu, Agu, Idemudia, & Ijomah, 2024). For example, various SMEs in manufacturing

have documented significant improvements in product quality and operational efficiency

by embedding AI solutions into their production lines (Peretz-Andersson, Tabares, Mikalef,

& Parida, 2024). Moreover, AI-focused startups have attracted substantial venture capital

interest, largely because their disruptive technologies can swiftly reshape established

markets (Bammens & Hünermund, 2021).

However, several barriers inhibit AI adoption among smaller firms. Chief among these

are  financial  and human  capital  constraints,  limiting  investment  in  robust  data

infrastructures and the recruitment of specialized AI talent. A McKinsey study identifies

resource  scarcity  as a  primary  challenge  specifically  facing  manufacturing  SMEs.

Additionally,  SMEs   often   lack   sufficient   high-quality   datasets  and   effective

data-management practices, both essential for training reliable AI models (Chui, Manyika,

Miremadi, Henke, Chung, Nel, & Malhotra, 2018; Lamarre, Smaje, & Zemmel, 2023).

Furthermore, successful digital transformation (DX) requires committed leadership and an

organizational culture supportive of experimentation. Yet, SMEs frequently  prioritize

immediate   revenue   generation   over   long-term   technological   competitiveness,

undervaluing AI’s strategic importance (Burnaev et  al., 2023). Reflecting this reality,

nearly half of small enterprises surveyed reported having no immediate plans for AI

adoption.

Ethical and risk management concerns pose additional hurdles. Smaller organizations

generally have less formal oversight mechanisms to guard against algorithmic bias, opaque

decision processes, or cybersecurity threats (Bughin, Hazan, Sree Ramaswamy, & Chu,

2017).  Nevertheless,  the  emergence  of  no-code  and  low-code  AI  platforms  and

cloud-based AI application programming interfaces (APIs) reduces the technical barrier to

implementing  AI. By leveraging these newer tools—often complemented by targeted

training programs, government subsidies, or open-source solutions—SMEs and startups can

more feasibly integrate AI into their operations (Khan, Taherdoost, Madanchian, Ouaissa,

El Hajjami, & Rahman, 2024). Thus, while AI holds considerable promise for bolstering

competitiveness and aligning with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) objectives,

clear strategies and external support remain vital for successful adoption.

2.2 Convergence of AI and ESG

Building on the discussion of AI adoption in SMEs and startups, the intersection of

artificial intelligence (AI) with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) objectives

underscores a broader paradigmatic shift in how organizations perceive and implement

sustainability.  Rather  than  viewing ESG  as a  peripheral  compliance  requirement,

companies  increasingly  recognize  AI  as a  strategic instrument  that can  streamline

operational processes while fostering ethical accountability. In line with stakeholder theory

(Freeman, 2010) and the triple bottom line (Elkington, 1997), ESG-driven initiatives are

no longer confined to risk mitigation; they also embody opportunities for shared value

creation (Porter & Kramer, 2011). This section examines the conceptual rationale behind

AI-ESG integration, explores domain-specific applications, highlights the role of emerging

digital technologies in augmenting ESG  efforts, and discusses  limitations and  ethical

considerations.

2.2.1. The Rationale for AI-ESG Convergence

The  growing  emphasis on  environmental,  social, and governance  (ESG)  standards,

reinforced by frameworks such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),

highlights a fundamental  shift toward aligning organizational success with  societal and

environmental objectives. Simultaneously,  artificial  intelligence  (AI) has emerged as a

transformative means to support these objectives through data-driven decision-making.

This convergence between AI and ESG involves strategically integrating AI’s predictive,

optimization,  and  automation  capabilities  with ESG’s  sustainability  goals  across

environmental, social, and governance domains. Specifically, AI helps operationalize ESG by

translating abstract sustainability goals into measurable outcomes. For example, predictive

modeling and real-time monitoring technologies enable firms to accurately track resource

use and  emissions,  turning  qualitative ESG commitments  into  quantifiable  indicators

(Bebbington & Unerman, 2018). This  capability  is  particularly valuable for small and

medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which often lack resources to effectively pursue ESG

initiatives (Li et al., 2025). Responsibly implemented AI can thus enhance efficiency, reduce

operational costs, and strengthen stakeholder trust by providing verifiable ESG data.

Conceptually, this AI-ESG integration aligns closely with dynamic capabilities theory

(Teece,  Pisano, &  Shuen,  1997),  which  highlights  organizations'  abilities  to  adapt

strategically  in dynamic  environments. By  leveraging  AI,  firms can  better  identify

ESG-related  risks and  opportunities,  seize data-informed  strategies, and reconfigure

processes to meet sustainability demands. However, successfully converging AI and ESG

requires proactive ethical leadership. The strategic value of AI depends not only on

performance  optimization  but  equally  on  embedding  transparency,  fairness,  and

accountability into organizational systems (Burnaev et al., 2023). Leaders must ensure AI

adoption aligns with ethical standards—such as the OECD AI Principles or the EU’s

Ethics  Guidelines  for  Trustworthy AI—to  prevent  biases,  exclusion,  or  unintended

consequences that might ultimately undermine ESG goals.

2.2.2. Domain-Specific Applications

In practice, AI’s impact on ESG dimensions manifests differently across environmental,

social, and governance domains. In the environmental sphere, AI-driven solutions—such as

machine learning models integrated with satellite imagery or Industrial Internet of Things

(IoT)  sensors—facilitate  real-time  tracking of  emissions,  predictive maintenance, and

adaptive energy management. In particular, these tools enable proactive interventions that

reduce waste and carbon footprints, as  illustrated by manufacturing firms achieving

significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions (Lim, 2024). Social applications are

equally expansive. AI can promote fairness in hiring and promotion by identifying potential

biases through advanced analytics, and improve workplace safety by monitoring employee

well-being in high-risk environments (Ghobakhloo et al., 2023).

In governance, anomaly detection algorithms help preempt financial misreporting and

fraud,  while  chatbots  and  other  automated  tools  promote  consistent,  transparent

stakeholder  engagement. These  domain-specific  applications  align  closely  with  the

resource-based view  (Barney,  1991),  highlighting how  intangible assets—such as AI

capabilities and reputational capital from ESG leadership—serve as critical sources of

sustained  competitive advantage  (Zeng,  Yunis,  Khalil, &  Mirza,  2024). To  illustrate

AI-driven ESG initiatives, <Table 1> summarizes key applications, outcomes, and relevant

theories.

Moreover, integrating AI with big data, IoT, and blockchain significantly enhances ESG

initiatives. IoT sensors in factories and logistics networks provide real-time data on energy

use, waste generation, and workplace safety. AI algorithms analyze this data instantly,

enabling timely responses to inefficiencies or risks. For example, textile manufacturers

can combine temperature and humidity sensor data with production analytics to optimize

energy consumption and minimize fabric waste, generating operational savings aligned

with shared value creation (Ministry of SMEs and Startups, 2025).

At the same time, blockchain technology offers a secure, tamper-resistant platform for

storing and verifying ESG-related information. This  is particularly beneficial in supply

chain contexts, where ethical sourcing and transparent recordkeeping are top priorities.

An AI-enabled system can detect anomalies in supplier data—indicating possible unethical

labor practices or incorrect emissions reporting—and automatically log these findings on

a blockchain ledger. This approach deters greenwashing and supports compliance with

emerging standards, such as Integrated Reporting and the Task Force on Climate-related

Financial Disclosures (Miglionico, 2022). Together, these emerging technologies enhance

the precision,  scalability, and credibility of ESG initiatives, opening new frontiers for

established corporations and resource-constrained SMEs.

2.2.3. Risks and Ethical Considerations

Despite its promise, AI-led ESG carries inherent challenges that must be addressed to

ensure equitable and sustainable outcomes. For SMEs and startups,  limited  financial

resources and human capital often hamper the development of robust AI infrastructures,

reflecting structural barriers recognized in resource dependence theory (Pfeffer; 1987;

Pfeffer & Salancik,  2015). Furthermore, data-related complexities—ranging from the

availability of  large,  high-quality datasets to stringent data privacy regulations—can

impede model accuracy and regulatory compliance.

Ethical risks also persist, particularly concerning algorithmic bias. If training data lack

diversity or reflect historical inequities, AI systems may perpetuate discriminatory patterns,

thereby undermining progress on the social dimension of ESG (Guan, Dong, & Zhao, 2022;

Minkkinen et al., 2024). Cybersecurity represents another critical area of concern, given

the extensive data interchange required by AI-driven ESG systems (Zeng et al., 2024).

As IoT sensors and blockchain networks expand, firms face heightened risks of data

breaches or malicious tampering, potentially compromising proprietary information and

undermining  public  trust  in ESG  disclosures (Minkkinen et  al.,  2024). Consequently,

organizations must strengthen data governance through secure frameworks and clear

accountability structures, such as cross-functional oversight committees, internal audits,

and adherence to standards like ISO 27001 for information security. In short, integrating

AI with ESG signals a strategic shift from compliance toward embedding sustainability into

core decision-making processes. By leveraging AI’s predictive and analytical capabilities,

firms  can  proactively  address  inefficiencies,  enhance  social  welfare,  and  ensure

transparent governance (Iyelolu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024).

2.3 Adopting AI for ESG versus Enhancing ESG in AI-Based Firms

Building on the previous analysis, this section explores two distinct yet complementary

strategic approaches: (1) adopting AI primarily to achieve ESG goals and (2) enhancing

ESG practices in firms with advanced AI  capabilities. Although both leverage AI for

sustainable outcomes,  their  motivations,  challenges, and  benefits  differ  significantly,

especially for SMEs and startups. The key differences between these strategies are

summarized in <Figure 1>.

<Figure 1> AI Adoption for ESG vs. ESG Enhancement in AI Firms

2.3.1. Strategy of Adopting AI for ESG

Effectively integrating AI into ESG initiatives requires a strategic approach addressing

three interrelated dimensions: data infrastructure, specialized talent, and organizational

culture.  First, organizations must develop robust data systems capable of accurately

capturing ESG-related metrics. Manufacturing firms, for instance, might deploy sensors to

track energy use and material waste, while financial institutions aggregate ESG indicators

across investment portfolios. Analyzing such datasets through machine learning and deep

learning  methods  can  provide  actionable  insights  for  strategic  decision-making

(Peretz-Andersson et al., 2024).

Second, successful AI-ESG integration depends on securing professionals with expertise

in both AI technologies and sustainability. Increasingly, firms are aligning analytics teams

closely with Chief Sustainability Officers (CSOs) or forming partnerships with external AI

specialists to bridge existing capability gaps  (Asif et  al., 2023). Third, cultivating an

ESG-centric  organizational  culture  is  essential.  Leaders must  actively champion  AI

adoption, clearly communicate its strategic importance, and allocate sufficient resources

for experimentation and learning. Although integrating AI involves iterative  trial and

error,  a  committed  leadership  approach  helps   institutionalize  data-driven  ESG

decision-making, ultimately enhancing operational efficiency and sustainability outcomes

(Florea & Croitoru, 2025).

While  the  initial  investment  in  technology,  talent, and  cultural change can be

substantial, organizations effectively adopting AI for ESG initiatives strengthen investor

trust  and  market  credibility  (Minkkinen  et   al.,  2024).  For  example,  traditional

manufacturers  using  AI-driven energy management systems can  significantly lower

carbon emissions and transparently report their progress to stakeholders (Ali, Motuzienė,

& Džiugaitė-Tumėnienė, 2024). SMEs facing resource constraints can begin by adopting

cloud-based AI solutions or partnering with external consultants, gradually scaling their

capabilities to achieve measurable ESG outcomes. Ultimately, aligning digital investment

strategies  with ESG governance  not  only advances  sustainability agendas  but  also

promotes long-term operational excellence (Khan et al., 2024).

2.3.2. AI-Based Companies Enhancing ESG Strategy

In contrast, organizations rooted in AI typically have ESG principles more intrinsically

embedded in their products. Because they already excel in data analytics and algorithmic

innovation, their ESG frameworks tend to be proactive and tightly integrated. First, these

companies often establish ethical AI guidelines to address potential biases, ensure data

privacy, and maintain transparency. For instance, a large-scale AI solution provider might

form an ethics committee to assess societal risks, publish transparent documentation, and

implement  oversight  mechanisms  that  strengthen  governance  accountability   (Li,

Hammoud, Itani, Khizbullin, & Ghanem, 2023).

Second, creating social and environmental value emerges as a strategic priority. By

developing carbon-tracking software or specialized ESG assessment tools, AI-driven firms

capitalize on their technical strengths while advancing sustainability objectives. Many

startups operate with a dual positioning: as a green tech company that attracts socially

conscious customers and investors. (Crocco et  al., 2024). Third, sustainable operations

represent a  critical dimension. Because AI companies often maintain extensive data

centers,  incorporating renewable energy  sources  or  offsetting  emissions  is key  to

long-term viability. Major technology enterprises like Microsoft and Google have publicly

committed to solar and wind power investments, supplemented by carbon credits, in

pursuit of carbon neutrality (Shrimali, 2022). They also adopt green procurement and

waste reduction practices, extending environmental criteria to suppliers and addressing

Scope 3 emissions*.

Finally, transparent data disclosure and stakeholder engagement ensure that AI-based

enterprises maintain consistent governance standards. Historically, technology companies

have been cautious in revealing proprietary information, but ESG pressures drive more

openness—including support for open-source  projects,  clear algorithmic  policies, and

publicly available model evaluations (Khan et  al., 2024; Miglionico, 2022). Early-stage

startups  also  benefit from  articulating  social  missions and  publishing ESG  reports,

reinforcing investor confidence and differentiating themselves in a competitive market

(Mansouri & Momtaz, 2022). By weaving ESG into their core strategies, AI-oriented firms

can more readily adapt to regulatory changes, attract mission-aligned capital, and sustain

a competitive edge through responsible innovation.

2.3.3. Comparing the Viewpoints of SMEs and Startups

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and startups rarely adopt standardized

approaches to ESG and AI  strategies.  Instead,  firm-specific factors such as growth

trajectories, resource availability, and strategic objectives shape their integration paths

(Spiess-Knafl, 2022). To highlight these differences clearly, <Table 2> compares ESG-led

AI and AI-led ESG  strategies, summarizing  distinct  operational  logics,  benefits, and

challenges.

Technology-oriented startups typically pursue AI-led ESG, leveraging their inherent

capabilities  in advanced  analytics and  algorithms. For these  firms,  integrating ESG

principles into existing AI infrastructure incurs minimal additional costs and positions them

strategically to attract sustainability-focused investors (Burnaev et al., 2023).

In contrast, traditional SMEs—particularly in manufacturing or construction—tend to

Each approach presents unique advantages and trade-offs. SMEs without strong digital

III. Strategic Models for ESG-AI Integration

Organizations typically adopt one of two strategic pathways to integrate environmental,

social, and governance (ESG)  criteria with  artificial  intelligence  (AI). An ESG-led AI

approach suits SMEs or traditional firms with limited technology, enabling incremental AI

adoption to achieve ESG targets. Conversely, an AI-led ESG strategy aligns best with

tech-focused startups or firms  proficient  in  AI, leveraging  existing competencies to

strengthen responsible practices. Drawing from resource-based theory (Barney, 1991) and

dynamic capabilities theory (Teece et al., 1997), this section systematically compares these

strategies, explores hybrid approaches, and provides practical guidance supported by

3.1 ESG-led AI Strategy Model

An  ESG-led  AI  approach  begins  by  evaluating  current ESG  performance  and

technological readiness. SMEs  typically assess environmental metrics such as energy

efficiency, carbon emissions, and waste management; social factors like labor practices

and community  involvement; and governance  aspects  including  internal  ethics and

compliance processes (Smith, Schäfer, & Bernstein, 2024). Based on this assessment, firms

conduct a gap analysis to pinpoint areas where targeted AI interventions can achieve

meaningful ESG improvements.

Implementing this strategy involves deploying specific AI  tools, such as IoT-driven

energy management, machine vision for optimized production, or NLP for employee

engagement  analytics  (Ali  et  al.,  2024; Crocco  et  al.,  2024). Given  limited  internal

expertise, SMEs  frequently leverage  external  partnerships  or  incrementally develop

in-house  AI  capabilities.  Essential  infrastructural elements  include cloud-based data

storage, secure governance frameworks, and real-time analytics capabilities. Pilot projects

typically focus on high-impact ESG areas—for example, predictive energy optimization or

sensor-based workplace safety monitoring—and are gradually scaled upon successful

outcomes (Rane et al., 2024).

Sustaining ESG-led AI  efforts requires  clearly defined KPIs, transparent AI-driven

reporting, strong leadership commitment, employee training, and continuous refinement of

AI applications (Blank, Sgambati, & Truelson, 2016). This approach effectively integrates

ESG  principles  into core business  operations,  ultimately strengthening  organizational

sustainability and competitiveness.

3.2 AI-led ESG Strategy Model

The AI-led ESG approach emphasizes embedding responsible AI (RAI) governance

structures to proactively manage ethical,  social, and governance risks (Lu, Zhu, Xu,

Whittle, Zowghi, & Jacquet, 2024), particularly in tech-focused SMEs and startups with

established AI infrastructure. Ethical oversight mechanisms, such as data governance

boards or ethics committees, address algorithmic bias, data privacy, and transparency

throughout AI deployment, strengthening stakeholder trust (Guan et al., 2022).

These AI-centric firms often deploy their capabilities directly toward significant social

and  environmental  challenges.  AI-driven  diagnostic  tools,  personalized  educational

technologies, environmental monitoring through computer vision, or predictive analytics

for disaster mitigation illustrate this proactive approach. Real-world examples include

deploying NLP  analytics  to measure  public  policy  sentiment  or  using drone-based

computer vision to monitor deforestation (Verma, 2022), each providing tangible societal

benefits and new market opportunities (Bebbington & Unerman, 2018).

Furthermore, sustainable operations are essential for AI-intensive organizations due to

their large computational demands. Companies like Google have harnessed AI to optimize

data center cooling systems, achieving approximately 40% energy savings (Karunakara

Malige & Ananth, 2024). Additional sustainability practices—such as renewable energy

sourcing, waste-heat recovery, and efficient computing architectures—underscore how

operational excellence can align with environmental responsibility (Miglionico, 2022; Smith

et al., 2024).

For these reasons, transparent, data-driven governance  is  critical for AI-led ESG

organizations. Automated ESG  reporting and  real-time  risk monitoring  help reduce

potential harms while enhancing responsiveness, and clear disclosure protocols bolster

trust among investors, consumers, and regulatory bodies. Effective crisis communication

and accountability measures reinforce ethical standards, ensuring AI’s transformative

power contributes to business success and societal benefit.

3.3 Comparative Analysis of ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG

Although both ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG approaches integrate ESG criteria with AI

technologies, they differ significantly in motivation and operational focus. ESG-led AI

adopts a top-down perspective, starting from clearly defined sustainability goals and

employing AI solutions to realize them. Conversely, AI-led ESG leverages existing AI

infrastructure, subsequently embedding ESG considerations into operations and ethics

frameworks (Chen et  al., 2024; Nishant et  al., 2020). Practical industry cases highlight

these strategic differences (Ministry of SMEs and Startups, 2025), as illustrated in <Figure 2>.

1. Manufacturing Industry (ESG-led AI): A metal parts producer introduced IoT sensors

and a predictive maintenance algorithm, reducing overall energy consumption by 20%,

minimizing raw material waste, and improving operational throughput.  Initially, limited

digital literacy and resistance to new technology required targeted training and external

partnerships. Over several months, the pilot project scaled across multiple production

lines, illustrating how a top-down ESG focus can drive steady, long-term improvements.

2. Textile Industry (ESG-led  AI): A garment manufacturing SME adopted AI-driven

demand forecasting and defect detection, cutting fabric waste by 10% and enhancing

quality control. These incremental gains fostered a more positive work environment, as

employees benefited from safer schedules and clearer performance metrics. This example

underscores how incremental AI adoption can effectively address both economic and

social dimensions of ESG.

3. Tech  Industry  (AI-led ESG): A data  analytics  startup  utilizes  natural language

processing  (NLP)  to  automate ESG  risk  assessments,  enhancing  transparency and

stakeholder communication. Meanwhile, Google’s AI-based data center optimizations

achieved up to 40% reductions in cooling energy, aligning operational efficiency with

environmental objectives. These examples show how preexisting AI infrastructures can

deliver  swift,  high-impact  results—provided  there  is  robust  ethical  oversight  and

stakeholder engagement to prevent unintended consequences (Kazachenok et al., 2023).

sections.title: IV. Conclusion
sections.content:
4.1 Summary

This  study has examined two  strategic models  for  integrating  sustainability and

technological innovation: ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG. Although both frameworks seek to

align environmental, social, and governance (ESG) principles with artificial intelligence

(AI), their starting points differ  significantly. ESG-led AI entails building responsible,

transparent AI  solutions to meet  stringent ESG requirements, making  it  particularly

suitable  for  organizations—often  small and medium-sized  enterprises (SMEs)—whose

digital infrastructures remain underdeveloped (Minkkinen et al., 2024; Peretz-Andersson,

et al., 2024) In contrast, AI-led ESG leverages well-established AI competencies to address

ESG challenges more immediately, favoring tech-driven interventions that can rapidly

scale. Viewed in tandem, these models underscore AI’s expanding function as a force

for resilience and long-term societal value, well beyond mere operational efficiency

<Figure 3>.

<Figure 3> Summary of ESG-Led AI and AI-Led ESG

From  a  policy  and  practical  perspective,  the  findings  highlight  three  critical

interventions to foster an enabling environment for both ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG.

First, tailored support for SMEs—through specialized training, consulting subsidies, or

targeted tax incentives—can alleviate the financial and human capital constraints they

frequently encounter. Such measures not only lower  initial adoption costs but  also

promote phased implementation of AI tools, ensuring that ESG objectives remain central

during digital transformation (Blank et al., 2016; He, 2024).

Second, establishing and enforcing robust AI ethics guidelines helps avert algorithmic

bias, data misuse, and opaque decision-making processes (Agapova & Garanina, 2024).

When developed collaboratively by governments, industry associations, and academic

institutions, these guidelines serve as guardrails that bolster public trust and steer AI

deployments toward equitable, socially beneficial outcomes (Iyelolu et al., 2024; Mansouri

& Momtaz, 2022).

Finally, mandatory ESG disclosure provides the transparency essential for effective

AI-driven analyses. By requiring firms to report on emissions,  social  initiatives, and

governance   practices,  policymakers  reduce   information  asymmetry,   discourage

greenwashing, and enable stakeholders to accurately evaluate corporate ESG performance

(Chui et  al., 2018; Kazachenok et  al., 2024). Operationally, ESG-led AI often involves

incrementally enhancing existing processes—such as energy management or supply-chain

monitoring—by integrating AI solutions that optimize resource usage, identify anomalies,

or  predict emerging  risks.  In contrast, AI-led ESG enables firms with advanced AI

capabilities to pursue more ambitious  initiatives, such as developing low-carbon data

centers or deploying predictive analytics for community health.

Despite these differences, the core message remains consistent: AI can become the

linchpin of ethical and sustainable corporate transformation, provided robust governance

structures, committed leadership, and transparent stakeholder engagement are in place.

Building on stakeholder theory (Freeman, 2010) and dynamic capabilities (Teece et  al.,

1997), the strategic models in this study demonstrate that embedding ESG within AI—and

AI within ESG can generate a virtuous cycle of innovation and accountability.

Moreover, recognizing the complementary nature of these two approaches underscores

an important theme: synergistic integration. Even tech-savvy startups can learn from

ESG-led AI’s  methodical  emphasis  on  ethics  and  responsible  governance,  while

traditional SMEs adopting ESG-led AI can benefit from the scalability and agility that

characterize AI-led ESG. Over time, organizations may transition between or combine

these  models,  forging  hybrid  strategies  that  unite  gradual  capacity-building  with

disruptive, high-impact solutions (Florea & Croitoru, 2025). This fluidity not only amplifies

ESG outcomes but also reinforces public trust, attracting mission-aligned investors and

galvanizing broader stakeholder support.

For SMEs  in  particular, external  policy  incentives and a step-by-step  integration

strategy can mitigate  financial and  technical  barriers, transforming short-term  pilot

programs into long-term competitive advantages (Khan et  al., 2024; Chui et  al., 2018).

Ultimately, whether an organization initiates its journey with ESG-led AI or AI-led ESG,

the end goal converges on responsible digital innovation—an imperative in an era where

environmental constraints, social well-being, and governance expectations are redefining

global  market  dynamics.  By  uniting  technological  excellence  with  sustainability

imperatives, firms can ensure that AI’s transformative capabilities not only enhance

operational efficiency but also foster equitable growth and ecological stewardship for

future generations (Bammens & Hünermund, 2021).

4.2 Limitation and Future Research

Despite the promise of ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG,  this study’s findings remain

conceptual  and  partially  illustrated  through  selective  case  examples  rather  than

comprehensive  empirical  data.  First, the  lack of  large-scale,  data-driven  validation

presents a key limitation. Researchers could undertake longitudinal or cross-sectional

studies in multiple industries to quantify how AI adoption directly or indirectly affects ESG

performance over time. Such analyses would elucidate best practices, uncover potential

trade-offs, and provide tangible evidence for policymakers and corporate strategists.

Second, an industry-specific focus dominated many existing discussions, spotlighting

sectors like finance and high-tech (Asif et al., 2023). Future research should explore how

these dual models function in diverse environments—including manufacturing, healthcare,

and the public sector—where operational processes and stakeholder complexities differ

markedly. Such breadth would deepen our understanding of the conditions under which

ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG thrive or falter.

Third, the rapid pace of  technological and regulatory change  calls  for  continual

updating of theoretical frameworks and governance mechanisms (Wu, Straub, & Liang,

2015). Dynamic  regulatory landscapes and emerging AI innovations—from federated

learning  to  quantum  computing—require  agile,  adaptive  strategies.  Scholars  and

practitioners may investigate how real-time policy adjustments and advanced governance

protocols could strengthen ethical oversight and ESG impacts (Nishant et al., 2020).

Finally, the combined implementation of ESG-led AI and AI-led ESG represents a

promising yet underexplored area for empirical study. Although theory suggests that

organizations applying both models simultaneously or sequentially may achieve superior

outcomes, systematic evaluations of this synergy relative to singular strategies remain

limited (Acquaah & Yasai-Ardekani, 2008). Empirical validation could guide organizations

in  effectively  integrating  responsible  AI  practices  with ESG  objectives,  informing

standards and advancing sustainable digital transformation. Exploring these opportunities

can enhance theoretical clarity on ESG–AI integration, offering practical, evidence-based

insights for policymakers, firms, and communities pursuing ethical and sustainable AI

adoption.
